$comment: THE canonical role source. tools/verify-task-contracts.mjs reads this file for the owner_role enum; nothing anywhere restates the list. A second hand-maintained enum is how a taxonomy drifts, and role-model.test.mjs fails if one appears. Roles describe AUTHORITY DOMAIN only - what kind of work this is and who may own it. They are orthogonal to risk (worst reach) and production_effect (maximum effect permitted), and a role NEVER grants permission to exceed a contract's allowed_paths, forbidden_paths, acceptance_criteria, stop_conditions, risk or production_effect.

roles.purpose: Owns learner-facing application behaviour and general product UI that is not story/content semantics, scheduler/database semantics, release/compliance authority, or repository automation authority.
roles.mental_model: How the learner moves through and interacts with the application.
authority: Onboarding and first-run product flows
Auth/account UX and application-level validation
Navigation, routing and the app shell
Generic learner-facing screens
Design-system components and tokens
Settings and feedback flows
Offline application behaviour and offline UI
General product state and interaction behaviour
non_authority: No story/vocabulary/curriculum/Reader semantic authority
No FSRS/scheduler/cards/schema/migration authority
No privacy-policy, compliance, store, native release or signing authority
No CI/workflow/task-control-plane authority
No live production mutation merely because a product flow consumes production data
owns_examples: Reworking the onboarding path so the first lesson comes before account creation
Fixing the sign-in form's email validation and its error copy
Adding a nav entry and its route
Adjusting a design token used across screens
Making the offline bar reflect a queued write
hand_off_examples: Changing how the reader matches vocabulary to text -> story-content
Changing what counts as due, or a cards/schema migration -> scheduler-db
Native Sign in with Apple provider configuration or entitlements -> privacy-release
Changing a required CI check or a workflow trigger -> workflow-authority

roles.purpose: Owns the learning material itself and the semantics that decide whether it is correct: stories, vocabulary and content integrity, Reader/matcher behaviour, and the generation and content tooling behind them.
roles.mental_model: What the learner reads and learns, and whether the lexical/content semantics are correct.
authority: Stories, seasons, chapters and their publication state
Vocabulary and content integrity, including readings and definitions
Reader and matcher semantics - how text is segmented and matched to known words
Story/vocabulary generation and content tooling, and their validators
Content-facing checks such as the published-story validator
non_authority: No FSRS/scheduler/cards/schema authority - content decides what is read, not what is scheduled
No general product UI, navigation or app-shell authority
No privacy, compliance, store or native release authority
No CI/workflow authority, including the workflows that run the content tooling
Not a general product-engineering role - ordinary application work belongs to product-app
owns_examples: Fixing a wrong pinyin reading in the HSK vocabulary
Changing how storyReading.js segments and matches CJK text
Adding a generation check that a story really contains its required words
Publishing a held chapter through the content tooling
hand_off_examples: Changing where a content workflow is allowed to push -> workflow-authority
Changing how a read story affects card scheduling -> scheduler-db
Redesigning the Stories shelf layout and navigation -> product-app
Deciding whether generated art may be described as AI-made in the Terms -> privacy-release

roles.purpose: Owns what the learning system knows, stores, schedules and counts: FSRS and scheduler semantics, cards and reviews, and database schema and migration work.
roles.mental_model: What the learning system knows, stores, schedules and counts.
authority: FSRS scheduling and its parameters
Card and review state, and the predicates over it (learned, mastered, due)
Database schema, migrations and the RPCs the app depends on
Progress, level and mastery accounting
The sync/outbox path that persists grading
non_authority: No story/vocabulary/content semantic authority
No general product UI, navigation or app-shell authority
No privacy, compliance, store or native release authority
No CI/workflow authority
Writing a migration is not permission to APPLY it - applying against production is its own task with its own production_effect
owns_examples: Changing the FSRS request retention or the learning-steps handling
Correcting what counts as due so Home and the session agree
Writing a migration that adds a column the app reads
Fixing the transactional grading RPC
hand_off_examples: Applying a migration against the live database -> a task with production_effect database, reviewed as such
Changing the flashcard screen's layout -> product-app
Changing which words a story is allowed to use -> story-content
Changing the CI job that runs the migration checks -> workflow-authority

roles.purpose: Owns what may legally and safely ship, and how native and store release authority is exercised: privacy, security and compliance, native release configuration, and App Store / Play release work.
roles.mental_model: What may legally/safely ship, and how native/store release authority is exercised.
authority: Privacy policy, terms, and compliance decisions
Security-sensitive configuration, credentials, signing and native identity-provider setup
Native release configuration and store metadata
App Store / Play identity requirements, submission and publication
Data-handling disclosures and privacy manifests
non_authority: No general product UI or app-flow authority - a sign-in SCREEN is product-app
No story/vocabulary/content semantic authority
No FSRS/scheduler/cards/schema authority
No generic CI/workflow authority - the native CI gate ARCHITECTURE is workflow-authority
Not the owner of every file that mentions authentication
owns_examples: Rewriting the privacy policy to match what the app actually stores
Configuring the Apple identity provider and its signing credentials
Filling in Data Safety answers for a store listing
Cutting a TestFlight or Play release
hand_off_examples: The sign-in screen's layout, validation and post-auth navigation -> product-app
Changing the native CI gate or required-check composition -> workflow-authority
Deleting a user's rows on request -> a task with production_effect database
Changing what the app stores in the first place -> scheduler-db or product-app, depending on the data

roles.purpose: Owns the repository automation and control-plane rules under which other work is built, checked, merged, and allowed to mutate repository state.
roles.mental_model: The repository rules under which work is checked, automated and merged.
authority: CI/workflow definitions and triggers
Required-check and gate composition
Workflow permissions and concurrency
Automation write paths and branch-safety rules
Task-contract infrastructure and validators
Repository-side branch-protection/ruleset specifications and their verification
Automation authority documentation and contract tests
non_authority: No product behaviour changes
No story/vocabulary/content semantics
No FSRS/scheduler semantics
No live production database mutation
No privacy-policy or product-compliance decisions
No app-store publication or signing authority
Must not grant itself production credentials or broaden its own task contract
owns_examples: Stopping a workflow from pushing to main, and proving it with a contract test
Composing an always-present gate job that is safe to require on main
Adding a validator and its specs to the task-contract infrastructure
Specifying the main ruleset and verifying it holds
hand_off_examples: Changing what a content workflow GENERATES -> story-content
Cutting the release the release workflow builds -> privacy-release
Writing the Playwright spec a gate runs -> qa
Fixing the app code a failing check exposed -> product-app, story-content or scheduler-db

roles.purpose: Independently exercises and verifies behaviour: Playwright and integration verification, screenshots, native/device verification, and reproduction work.
authority: Playwright and integration test implementation
Screenshots and visual baselines
Native and on-device verification
Reproducing reported failures and narrowing them to a cause
Test fixtures and mocks that support verification
non_authority: Does not define which gates are required or how verification is wired into repository authority - that is workflow-authority
No product, content, scheduler, privacy or release implementation authority
Reproducing a bug is not authority to fix it in the owning domain
No live production mutation
owns_examples: Writing a Playwright spec for the onboarding flow
Reproducing a reported crash on a real device and narrowing it
Refreshing a visual baseline after an approved design change
Adding a fixture that makes an integration path testable
hand_off_examples: Making that spec a required check, or changing the e2e workflow trigger -> workflow-authority
Fixing the onboarding bug the spec found -> product-app
Deciding a failing visual baseline is an intended design change -> product-app
Verifying a store build is signable -> privacy-release

roles.purpose: Independently judges an implementation against its contract and diff, from fresh context. Review only.
roles.mental_model: Independently judges the implementation against the contract and diff.
authority: Reading code, task contracts, diffs and history
Running verification commands to check claims
Judging whether acceptance_criteria are genuinely met
Reporting findings, and refusing to sign off
non_authority: MUST NOT implement the task being reviewed - see the implementer/reviewer separation below
No authority to relax acceptance_criteria, widen allowed_paths, or re-seal a contract to fit what was built
No production mutation
No merge authority - integration is integrator's
owns_examples: Reading a diff against its contract and reporting where they disagree
Running the contract's verification commands and reporting the real result
Refusing sign-off because an acceptance criterion is unmet
hand_off_examples: Fixing what the review found -> the implementing role that owns that domain
Deciding the criterion itself was wrong -> the task's owner, as a contract change with a visible re-seal
Merging the approved work -> integrator

roles.purpose: Integrates already-approved work: resolves integration conflicts and runs the defined gates, without redefining requirements or gates.
roles.mental_model: Integrates already-approved work without redefining requirements or gates.
authority: Merging and rebasing approved work
Resolving integration conflicts
Running already-defined gates and reporting their result
Sequencing merges so dependent work lands in order
non_authority: Must not silently change product requirements or acceptance_criteria
Must not define, weaken, or bypass gates - that is workflow-authority
No implementation authority in any product domain
No production mutation
owns_examples: Merging main into a stale approved branch and resolving the conflict
Running the gates on a combined result before landing it
Sequencing two approved PRs whose migrations must land in order
hand_off_examples: A conflict where both sides changed the same behaviour -> the owning role decides
A gate that is wrong or too slow -> workflow-authority
Work that is not yet approved -> reviewer

separation.implementer_is_not_reviewer: The implementer of a task cannot also serve as its independent fresh-context reviewer. Independence is the whole value of the review: an agent that judges its own work brings the same blind spots and the same reading of the contract that produced the work. This is a SEMANTIC rule recorded here and asserted by role-model.test.mjs. Nothing enforces it at runtime yet - there is no reviewer agent and no dispatch layer - so it currently binds whoever assigns the work.
separation.role_never_overrides_contract: A role is an authority DOMAIN, never a permission to exceed the task contract. No role grants the ability to modify paths outside allowed_paths, to touch forbidden_paths, to relax acceptance_criteria, to ignore stop_conditions, or to exceed the contract's risk or production_effect. Where a role and a contract disagree, the contract is narrower and the contract wins.
